diagrams.title: Take a permit, call, give it back

elements.label: Netflix Hystrix
elements.sub: thread pools or semaphores · maintenance mode

edges.label: contains it while the breaker decides

shots.engineer: A ship's hull is divided by watertight walls called bulkheads. If the hull is holed, only one compartment floods, and the ship stays afloat. Software needs the same thing. Here is a web app that calls payments, the catalogue and recommendations. Every one of those calls runs on threads from a single shared pool of two hundred. Nothing is broken yet.
shots.executive: Ships are split into watertight compartments so one leak cannot sink them. This web app has no compartments: every call shares one pool of workers.

shots.title: Exhaustion
shots.engineer: Now payments gets slow: thirty seconds per answer. At a hundred checkouts a second, each holding a thread for thirty seconds, you would need three thousand threads. The pool has two hundred, so it is gone in about two seconds. Now browsing fails, and recommendations fail, although both services are perfectly healthy. One slow dependency has drained a resource that everything shared.
shots.executive: When payments slows down, waiting checkouts use up every worker within seconds, and pages that never touch payments stop working too.

shots.title: Bigger pool
shots.engineer: The obvious fix is a bigger pool. Make it a thousand threads. But the arithmetic has not changed: a hundred checkouts a second, each waiting thirty seconds, still needs three thousand. A thousand threads are busy after ten seconds instead of two. Meanwhile every extra thread costs memory, and sends yet another call to the service that is already struggling. A bigger shared pool only delays the outage.
shots.executive: Adding more workers only buys a few seconds, costs memory, and piles more load on the struggling service.

shots.title: Partition
shots.engineer: The bulkhead pattern gives each dependency its own compartment. Calls to payments may use at most twenty-five permits; the catalogue gets fifty; recommendations get ten. Each bulkhead is a limit on how many calls to that one dependency can be in flight at once. If payments slows down, it can only ever hold twenty-five of the caller's threads. The rest stay free for everything else.
shots.executive: Each dependency gets its own fixed share of workers, so trouble with one can only use up its own share.

card.heading: Two ways to build a compartment
points: Thread-pool isolation | Semaphore isolation
Call runs on the bulkhead's own threads | Call runs on the caller's thread
Caller can time out and walk away | Caller waits until the call returns
A thread hand-off: Hystrix measured about 9 ms at p99 | Almost free: just a counter
Resilience4j ThreadPoolBulkhead | Resilience4j Bulkhead, Polly ConcurrencyLimiter

shots.engineer: There are two ways to build a compartment. Thread-pool isolation runs each call on the bulkhead's own small pool, so the caller can give up after a timeout and walk away. It costs a hand-off between threads: Netflix measured about nine milliseconds at the ninety-ninth percentile. Semaphore isolation is just a counter of permits. It is almost free, but the call runs on the caller's thread, so a stuck call keeps that thread until it returns.
shots.executive: A compartment can be its own small team of workers, which can abandon slow work, or a simple head count, which is cheaper but cannot.

shots.title: Permits
shots.engineer: Step by step. The web app takes a permit from the payments bulkhead, leaving twenty-four. The call goes out with its own timeout, payments answers, and the permit is returned. Now suppose twenty-five calls are already in flight. The twenty-sixth finds no permit and is rejected straight away, and the fallback tells the user their payment is pending. Twenty-five is Resilience4j's default limit, and its default wait for a permit is zero.
shots.executive: Each call takes a ticket and hands it back when done. When the tickets run out, new calls are turned away at once with a sensible fallback.

shots.title: Payments full
shots.engineer: Now replay the outage. Payments slows to thirty seconds. Its twenty-five permits fill within a fraction of a second, and every further charge is rejected and sent to the fallback. Rejections show up in the metrics, so operators see the compartment flooding. Meanwhile browsing still goes through the catalogue bulkhead, which is untouched. Checkout is degraded; the rest of the site is fine.
shots.executive: When payments slows down, only checkout is affected and users get a clear message. Browsing and everything else keep working.

card.heading: When a bulkhead is full
points: Reject fast: fail in microseconds, not in thirty seconds
Or queue, with a small bound, to absorb a short burst
Answer from a fallback the user can live with
Put a timeout inside it, or permits never come back

shots.engineer: When a bulkhead is full you have three choices. Reject straight away, which is fast and honest. Queue the call, but only in a small, bounded queue that absorbs a short burst; an unbounded queue is just a slower way to run out of memory. And answer from a fallback the user can accept. One more trap: the call inside the bulkhead needs a timeout, or a hung dependency keeps its permits for ever.
shots.executive: A full compartment should say no quickly, queue only a little, and give users a sensible fallback. Without timeouts, it never empties.

card.heading: Sizing a bulkhead: Little's law
points: 100 / s | peak calls when healthy
0.2 s | 99th-percentile latency
20 | calls in flight (100 × 0.2)
25 | with breathing room

shots.engineer: How big should each compartment be? Little's law says the average number of calls in flight equals the arrival rate times the time each one takes. Hystrix's guidance turns that into a rule: peak requests per second when healthy, times ninety-ninth percentile latency in seconds, plus some breathing room. So a hundred calls a second at two hundred milliseconds is twenty in flight; call it twenty-five. Keep it as small as that, because a small pool is what sheds load.
shots.executive: Size each compartment from how busy the dependency is and how long it normally takes, plus a little headroom, and no more.

card.heading: What it costs
points: Choice | Trade-off
Small or large pool | Small sheds load early; large leaves idle capacity
Reject or queue | Rejecting is fast; a bounded queue absorbs bursts but adds wait
Per dependency or per tenant | Dependency stops slow services; tenant stops noisy neighbours
Many pools | Each is another number to tune, watch and revisit

shots.engineer: Bulkheads cost something. Capacity reserved for one compartment sits idle while another is starved, so you use resources less efficiently. Every pool is another number to tune, monitor and revisit as traffic changes. You choose what to partition by: per dependency stops a slow service; per tenant or per customer stops a noisy neighbour. Microsoft's advice is to skip the pattern when that inefficiency or the added complexity is not worth it.
shots.executive: Compartments waste some capacity and add settings to manage. Use them where one failure spreading would really hurt.

shots.title: Cells
shots.engineer: The same idea scales up to whole systems. In a cell-based architecture, each cell is a complete copy of the workload, and a thin router sends each customer to one cell. A poison request from customer A only hurts cell one; customer B carries on. Shuffle sharding goes further: give each customer a random pair of eight workers, and there are twenty-eight different pairs, so one bad customer affects about one twenty-eighth of the others.
shots.executive: Large platforms split whole systems into independent cells, so a bad customer or a bad release only affects a small slice of users.

shots.title: Implementations
shots.engineer: In the wild. Netflix's Hystrix made per-dependency thread pools famous; it is now in maintenance mode, and Netflix points new projects to Resilience4j, which offers a semaphore Bulkhead and a ThreadPoolBulkhead. In dotnet, Polly version eight replaced its bulkhead with a concurrency limiter. Kubernetes gives each container CPU and memory limits, and each namespace a resource quota. And Amazon's Route fifty-three gives each domain its own shuffle shard of four virtual name servers out of two thousand and forty-eight.
shots.executive: Every major platform has bulkheads, from Java and dotnet libraries to Kubernetes limits and Amazon's cell-based services.

shots.title: Neighbours
shots.engineer: Its neighbours. A timeout is what gives a permit back when a call hangs. A circuit breaker stops calling a failing dependency; the bulkhead contains the damage while the breaker is still counting failures. Retries take permits too, so they must respect the limit. A fallback is what the user sees when the compartment is full. And rate limiting is easily confused with it: a rate limiter caps requests per second, a bulkhead caps calls in flight at once.
shots.executive: Bulkheads work with timeouts, circuit breakers and fallbacks. Rate limiting caps how often; a bulkhead caps how many at once.

card.heading: Recap
points: Partition resources so one failure cannot drain them all
Size each compartment: throughput × latency, plus headroom
When full, reject fast and fall back; never wait for ever

shots.engineer: Three things to remember. Partition your threads, connections and capacity, so one slow dependency or one noisy customer cannot drain what everyone shares. Size each compartment from throughput times latency, plus a little headroom, and no bigger. And when a compartment is full, reject fast and fall back, rather than letting callers wait for ever.
shots.executive: Split resources into compartments. Size them deliberately. When one fills, say no quickly and fall back.

meta.blurb: Partition threads, connections and capacity so one failing dependency or tenant cannot sink the rest.
